title: wait()/notify() vs Condition.await()/signal(): monitor wait-set vs multiple Conditions
keyPoints: wait()/notify() are Object methods used inside synchronized blocks; each object has one wait-set.
Condition.await()/signal() are used with ReentrantLock; each lock can have multiple Conditions (multiple wait-sets).
With one wait-set, notify() may wake the wrong type of thread (a producer instead of a consumer).
Multiple Conditions allow targeted wake-ups: notEmpty.signal() wakes only consumers, notFull.signal() wakes only producers.
Both require the wait to be in a while loop due to spurious wake-ups and stolen conditions.
Condition also provides awaitUninterruptibly() and await(timeout, unit) for more precise control.

s1_definition.oneliner: wait()/notify() uses a single wait-set per object (may wake wrong thread), while Condition.await()/signal() supports multiple wait-sets per lock for targeted wake-ups.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **wait()/notify()** – methods on `Object`, used inside `synchronized`. `wait()` releases the monitor lock and enters the object's single wait-set. `notify()` wakes one thread from that set. `notifyAll()` wakes all.
- **Condition** – obtained via `ReentrantLock.newCondition()`. `await()` releases the lock and enters the Condition's wait-set. `signal()` wakes one thread from that specific Condition.
- **Single vs multiple wait-sets** – with wait/notify, producers and consumers share one wait-set. `notify()` may wake a producer when only a consumer is needed. With Conditions, each type has its own wait-set.
- **Spurious wake-ups** – both mechanisms can experience spurious wake-ups. Always use a `while` loop around `wait()` or `await()`.
s1_definition.analogy: wait/notify is one waiting room for everyone. When you shout "NEXT", you might wake a withdrawal customer when only a deposit customer is needed. notifyAll() wakes all 50 people, but only 1 needs to act. Condition creates separate waiting rooms: deposit room and withdrawal room. Shout in the deposit room and only deposit customers wake up. Efficient and targeted.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  wait/notify (ONE wait-set):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Object Monitor                   │
  │  Wait-Set: [P1, P2, C1, C2, C3] │  mixed!
  │  notify() wakes ANY one thread   │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  Condition (MULTIPLE wait-sets):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ReentrantLock                    │
  │  notFull:  [P1, P2]             │  producers only
  │  notEmpty: [C1, C2, C3]         │  consumers only
  │  notFull.signal()  → wakes P1   │  targeted!
  │  notEmpty.signal() → wakes C1   │  targeted!
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`wait()`/`notify()` are the classic thread communication mechanism, but they have a fundamental limitation: each object has only one wait-set. When producers and consumers share that set, `notify()` may wake the wrong type of thread, and `notifyAll()` wakes all threads wastefully.

`Condition` objects (from `ReentrantLock.newCondition()`) solve this by providing multiple wait-sets per lock. `notEmpty.signal()` wakes only a consumer. `notFull.signal()` wakes only a producer. Zero wasted wake-ups.

Remember one sentence: use Condition for targeted wake-ups with separate wait-sets per condition, and always wrap await() in a while loop.
